feedback.problem: The equation of a curve is ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$ The normal line at the point $(-3,\,1)$ on the curve intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(-3,\,1).$  Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x-6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x}{-6y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(-3,\,1)$ is 

 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & ={(\frac{x}{3y})}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is ${m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-1}=1.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(-3,\,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-1) & =1(x+3) \\ y & =(x+3)+1 \\ y & =x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+4 \\ 0 & =x+4 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-4,\,0).$
